questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. What an ongoing role adds
questions.question: A Senegalese telecom's board makes its chief audit executive permanently responsible for the data privacy office. Which step do the Standards require MOST specifically because the role is ongoing?

options.A: Set a plan to hand the role back to management
options.B: Keep third-party assurance until 12 months after the role ends
options.C: Write the role and its safeguards into the internal audit charter
options.D: Advise the board and senior management on suitable safeguards

questions.key_concept: An ongoing role beyond internal auditing must be written into the charter: its responsibilities, the nature of the work and the safeguards.
questions.pre_read: Sort the four steps into three piles: any such role, a temporary role, an ongoing role.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1 separates two cases. For a role beyond internal auditing that continues, the chief audit executive must write the responsibilities, the nature of the work and the safeguards into the internal audit charter, which the board approves. Advising the board and senior management on safeguards, the closest choice, is required for every such role, whatever its length. The hand-back plan and the 12 months after the role ends belong to a temporary role.

wrong_explanations.A: A plan to return the duties to management is required when the role is temporary. This role is permanent, so there is nothing to hand back.
wrong_explanations.B: Another route to assurance is needed here too, but the 12 months after the role ends is the temporary-role rule. An ongoing role has no end date.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: advice on safeguards is a must here too, but for any role that could impair independence, temporary or ongoing. It is not what the role's length adds.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a hand-back plan belongs to a temporary role, and B, because assurance until 12 months after the end is also a temporary-role rule.
Final two: C beats D because advice on safeguards is required for every role beyond internal auditing; the step tied to an ongoing role is recording it in the charter.
Exam cue: for a role beyond internal auditing, read the duration first. Ongoing: charter and another route to assurance. Temporary: third-party assurance, 12 months after, and a hand-back plan.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Declining to rely on second-line work
questions.question: A Kenyan mobile-money firm's finance director wants internal audit to rely on compliance's agent-monitoring tests, which covered five of 900 agents and left nothing on file. What is the chief audit executive's BEST course?

options.A: Decline to rely on the tests and have internal auditors retest
options.B: Rely on the tests and document the basis for doing so
options.C: Rely on the tests and leave their conclusions with compliance
options.D: Raise the lack of coordination with senior management, then the board

questions.key_concept: Reliance is the chief audit executive's choice, made after evaluating the other provider's work. Work too weak to support conclusions is retested or redone.
questions.pre_read: A basis for reliance has to exist before it can be documented. Would these tests support a conclusion on 900 agents?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.5 asks the chief audit executive to consider relying on other providers, not to rely on them, and leaves that executive responsible for internal audit's conclusions. Its considerations add that, after evaluating the work, the chief audit executive may decide it cannot be relied on; internal auditors then retest or do the work themselves. Documenting a basis, the closest choice, is the rule when reliance is justified. Here there is none.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a documented basis is required when internal audit relies on another provider. Five agents out of 900, with nothing kept on file, give no sound basis to record.
wrong_explanations.C: Responsibility for internal audit's conclusions stays with the chief audit executive, whoever's work they rest on. It cannot be passed to compliance.
wrong_explanations.D: A coordination concern is raised with senior management first, then the board if needed, once coordination proves out of reach. The issue here is the quality of the work.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the chief audit executive stays responsible for internal audit's conclusions, and D, because the problem is weak testing, not a failure to coordinate.
Final two: A beats B because a basis must exist before it is documented; tests of five agents with nothing on file are retested, not relied on.
Exam cue: coordinate with every assurance provider, but rely only after evaluating the work. Saving effort is a reason to consider reliance; only work that holds up is a basis for it.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Whose follow-up is it
questions.question: The three-person internal audit function of a Norwegian fish farm is offered four standing tasks. Which task would MOST clearly be a second-line duty that could impair its independence?

options.A: Reviewing management's risk register when updating its own audit universe
options.B: Running the follow-up of actions from management's risk reviews
options.C: Consolidating the assurance providers' results into one report for the board
options.D: Running the follow-up of actions from its own engagements

questions.key_concept: Internal audit follows up actions from its own engagements. By The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management, it must not own management's follow-up.
questions.pre_read: Two options look alike. For each task, ask whose actions are being chased and who would answer if they slipped.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management draws the line by ownership. Internal audit monitors whether actions agreed in its own engagements are carried out, keeps its audit universe and brings assurance results together; all three serve its own planning and reporting. Chasing the actions from management's risk reviews is management's follow-up, which the statement says internal audit must not own. Following up its own engagements, the closest choice, is what Standard 15.2 requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Using management's risk information to keep its own audit universe current is part of planning internal audit's work. Internal audit reads the register; it does not run it.
wrong_explanations.C: The statement lists coordinating and consolidating assurance results among internal audit's own activities. It gives the board one picture without owning anyone's controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it looks the same, but these actions come from internal audit's own engagements. Confirming they were implemented is required by Standard 15.2.

tips: Eliminate: A, because reading management's risk register to update the audit universe serves internal audit's own planning, and C, because consolidating assurance results is listed among internal audit's own activities.
Final two: B beats D because internal audit confirms actions from its own engagements, while actions from management's risk reviews are management's to follow up.
Exam cue: when two tasks look alike, ask who owns the process. Internal audit may track its own results; running management's tracking makes it part of what it audits.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. What conformance is measured against
questions.question: Internal auditor Petra finds that a Slovak rail operator's internal audit function meets every requirement of a standard but skips a practice in its considerations for implementation. How should Petra BEST treat the skipped practice?

options.A: As a departure the chief audit executive must document and explain
options.B: As an essential condition the board may agree to set aside
options.C: As a preferred practice that conformance does not depend on
options.D: As nonconformance to disclose in each final engagement communication

questions.key_concept: Conformance is measured against a standard's requirements. Considerations for implementation describe preferred or optional practice, so skipping one needs no documented departure.
questions.pre_read: Which part of a standard uses 'must', and which uses 'should' or 'may'? Decide that before judging the gap.
questions.correct_explanation: Each standard has requirements, which use 'must', and considerations for implementation, which use 'should' for preferred practice and 'may' for optional practice. The function meets every requirement, so it conforms and the skipped practice calls for nothing more. Documenting and explaining a departure, the closest choice, is what Standard 4.1 asks of the chief audit executive when a requirement cannot be met. No requirement is unmet here.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: when a requirement cannot be met, the chief audit executive records and reports what happened, what was done instead, its effect and why. Every requirement is met here.
wrong_explanations.B: Essential conditions are the board's and senior management's part in Domain III. Agreeing that one is unnecessary applies to those, not to a preferred practice in the considerations.
wrong_explanations.D: A final communication discloses nonconformance when an engagement was not carried out in line with the Standards. Skipping a preferred practice is not nonconformance.

tips: Eliminate: B, because setting a condition aside by agreement applies to essential conditions, and D, because disclosure in a final communication is for an engagement that did not conform.
Final two: C beats A because documenting a departure is required when a requirement cannot be met; a skipped 'should' or 'may' leaves conformance intact.

Exam cue: check which part of the standard the practice sits in. Requirements bind; considerations describe preferred or optional practice; essential conditions belong to the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. A bonus scheme and the conditions for effectiveness
questions.question: A Moroccan retailer's chief audit executive, who reports directly to the board, ties auditors' bonuses to cost savings their findings impose on audited units. Which condition for effective internal auditing does this MOST directly threaten?

options.A: Internal auditors who assess without bias from their own interests
options.B: A function positioned independently, with accountability to the board
options.C: Work performed by professionals with the right competencies
options.D: Unrestricted access to records, personnel and physical property

questions.key_concept: Effective internal auditing needs auditors free from undue influence. Pay tied to outcomes in audited units threatens that, whatever the reporting line.
questions.pre_read: Is the weak point where the function sits, or what could sway each auditor's judgment?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain I ties effective internal auditing to three conditions; the third is internal auditors who are free from undue influence and judge objectively. A bonus that grows with the savings forced on audited units gives each auditor a personal stake in the findings, and Standard 2.2's considerations name such pay as a possible impairment of objectivity. Positioning, the closest choice, is sound here: the function answers directly to the board.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: independence is about where the function sits. The chief audit executive reports directly to the board, and no manager outside the function set this scheme.
wrong_explanations.C: Competence is a separate condition. Nothing in the facts suggests the auditors lack knowledge or skill; the scheme works on their motives.
wrong_explanations.D: Access to records, people and property comes with the function's authority. No access has been restricted, and access is not one of Domain I's three conditions.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the scheme changes motives and not skills, and D, because access is part of the function's authority and has not been restricted.
Final two: A beats B because the reporting line to the board is intact; the bonus sways each auditor's own judgment, which is objectivity, a matter of the person.
Exam cue: ask what the fact changes. A reporting line or an outside restriction touches independence; a personal interest, tie or reward touches an auditor's objectivity.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. Which required part settles a dispute
questions.question: A division head at an Ethiopian flower exporter insists the internal audit function answers to the finance director alone. Which required part of the charter should internal auditor Selam cite to settle this MOST directly?

options.A: The Purpose of Internal Auditing
options.B: The commitment to follow the Standards
options.C: The mandate, with its scope and types of services
options.D: The function's position and reporting relationships

questions.key_concept: The charter must state the function's organizational position and reporting relationships, as the board has determined them. That part answers who the function reports to.
questions.pre_read: List the four things every charter must state. Which one says where the function sits and to whom it answers?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.2 has the charter state at least four things: the Purpose of Internal Auditing, the commitment to the Standards, the mandate, and the function's organizational position and reporting relationships. Standard 7.1 adds that the board determines those relationships and the chief audit executive records them in the charter. That settles whom the function answers to. The mandate, the closest choice, says what the function may do, not where it reports.

wrong_explanations.A: The purpose section says why internal auditing exists and what it gives the board and management. It does not set out a reporting line.
wrong_explanations.B: The commitment to the Standards binds the function to professional requirements. It would matter in a dispute about how the work is done, not about who the function reports to.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the mandate gives authority, role and responsibilities, with scope and services. It settles what the function may review, not whom it reports to.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the purpose states why internal auditing exists, and B, because the commitment to the Standards concerns how the work is done.
Final two: D beats C because the mandate says what the function may do, while position and reporting relationships say where it sits and to whom it answers.
Exam cue: match the dispute to the charter part. Why we exist: purpose. How we work: the Standards. What we may do: the mandate. Whom we answer to: reporting relationships.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. The discussion still missing before the vote
questions.question: A Sri Lankan tea broker's audit committee has discussed chief audit executive Nimali's proposed charter and votes next week; the chief executive and finance director have not seen it. What should Nimali do FIRST?

options.A: Present the final draft to the audit committee for approval
options.B: Discuss the proposed charter with senior management
options.C: Ask the chief executive to approve the proposed charter
options.D: Agree with the committee how often to reaffirm the charter

questions.key_concept: Before approval, the chief audit executive must discuss a proposed charter with the board and senior management. Senior management gives input and does not approve.
questions.pre_read: Two groups must hear the proposed charter before anyone votes. Which group has not been heard yet?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 6.2 a proposed charter is talked through with senior management as well as the board before approval, so the text matches what each group understands and expects of the function. The committee has had its discussion; the executives have not, so theirs comes first. Presenting the final draft for approval, the closest choice, is the usual step once both have been heard. Senior management gives input; approval stays with the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a final draft usually goes to a board meeting for approval, but that step follows senior management's discussion of the proposed text, which has not happened.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management discusses the proposed charter and gives input. Approval is the board's; an executive approves a charter where that person acts as the governing body.
wrong_explanations.D: Agreeing how often to review and reaffirm the charter is preferred practice once a charter is in place. It does not replace the missing discussion.

tips: Eliminate: C, because senior management gives input and does not approve the charter, and D, because agreeing a review frequency is preferred practice for an approved charter.
Final two: B beats A because the discussion with senior management is a requirement that comes before approval; presenting the final draft for the vote would skip it.
Exam cue: for the charter, think 'discuss with two, approve by one'. Check that the board and senior management have each discussed the text before the board votes.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. What a charter amendment needs
questions.question: Chief audit executive Abla maintains a Ghanaian brewery's charter and wants to add advisory services to the types of services it lists; senior management supports this. Which step does the amendment MOST clearly still need?

options.A: A report of the charter change in the board's next update
options.B: The board's approval of the charter in its amended form
options.C: A review of the change with the board, without a vote
options.D: The board's acknowledgment that independence may be impaired

questions.key_concept: The board approves the charter, including its scope and types of services. A change needs that approval too; reporting the change is not enough.
questions.pre_read: Maintaining a document and approving it are different jobs. Who approved the charter in the first place?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.1 has the mandate recorded in the charter, which the board approves, and its essential conditions add that this approval covers which services the function offers. Adding advisory services changes that content, so the amended charter goes back to the board. Reporting the change, the closest choice, is also required of the chief audit executive under Standard 8.1, but telling the board is not the same as its approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the chief audit executive does report changes affecting the charter to the board and senior management, but a report informs the board; it does not approve the change.
wrong_explanations.C: Review without a vote fits the internal audit strategy, which is reviewed with the board and senior management. The charter and changes to it are approved.
wrong_explanations.D: The board acknowledges an impairment when it approves a role beyond internal auditing for the chief audit executive. Advisory services are internal audit services.

tips: Eliminate: C, because review with no vote is the rule for the strategy and not the charter, and D, because advisory services are not a role beyond internal auditing.
Final two: B beats A because the charter's types of services are board-approved content; reporting a change keeps the board informed but does not approve it.
Exam cue: sort the board's verbs. It approves the charter, the plan, the budget and the resource plan; it reviews the strategy; it receives reports on the rest.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. A request labeled advisory
questions.question: An Estonian bank's treasury head asks internal audit for 'light advisory work' ending in a letter to the board stating that treasury controls are effective. How should internal auditor Maarja BEST classify the request?

options.A: Advisory: its nature and scope are agreed with the treasury head
options.B: Advisory: the treasury head wants light work without formal findings
options.C: Assurance: the board has asked for the work itself
options.D: Assurance: the letter gives a conclusion on control effectiveness

questions.key_concept: The deliverable decides the service. A statement that controls are effective is assurance; advisory work gives advice and no assurance, whatever the request is called.
questions.pre_read: Look past the label on the request. What will the letter tell its reader, and would the reader rely on it?
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary treats assurance as a statement meant to raise confidence in how something is governed and controlled, measured against criteria, and advisory services as advice without assurance. A letter telling the board that treasury controls are effective is such a statement, so the work must be planned as assurance. Agreeing scope with the requester, the closest choice, is how advisory work is set up; it cannot turn a conclusion on effectiveness into advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: advisory nature and scope are agreed with the requester, but the requested letter gives assurance. How the scope is settled does not change that.
wrong_explanations.B: Advisory work may go without evidence-based findings by agreement. A statement that controls are effective needs criteria and evidence, so 'light' work cannot support it.
wrong_explanations.C: The treasury head made the request, not the board. And who asks for work, or reads its result, does not classify it; what the letter states does.

tips: Eliminate: B, because going without findings is possible where no assurance is given, and C, because the treasury head made the request and the requester does not decide the type.
Final two: D beats A because advisory work gives no assurance; a letter concluding that controls are effective is assurance, however its scope was agreed.
Exam cue: classify by what is delivered, not by the label or the requester. A conclusion against criteria is assurance; ideas and input are advice.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. What an advisory agreement cannot waive
questions.question: A Japanese paper mill's plant manager wants informal comments on a draft maintenance procedure, and internal auditor Kaito agrees to keep the work as light as the Standards allow. Which step remains MOST clearly required?

options.A: Approval of the objectives and scope by the chief audit executive
options.B: A formal, documented assessment of the procedure's risks
options.C: Identification of criteria to evaluate the procedure against
options.D: Gathering of evidence to develop engagement findings

questions.key_concept: By agreement, advisory work may drop a formal risk assessment, criteria and evidence-based findings. Approval of objectives and scope by the chief audit executive remains.
questions.pre_read: Three planning and fieldwork steps carry an exception for advisory work in the Standards. Which listed step has no such exception?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards apply to advisory work unless a standard says otherwise, and three say so: depending on the agreement, a formal documented risk assessment (Standard 13.2), evaluation criteria (Standard 13.4) and evidence gathered to develop findings (Standard 14.2) may not be needed. Standard 13.3 has no such exception, so the chief audit executive, or a delegated supervisor, still approves the objectives and scope. The formal risk assessment, the closest choice, is required for assurance work.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: assurance work needs a documented risk assessment. For advisory work Standard 13.2 lets a formal, documented one be left out by agreement; understanding the activity stays.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 13.4 says identifying evaluation criteria may not be necessary for advisory services, depending on the agreement. Informal comments on a draft can do without them.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 14.2 lets advisory work go without evidence gathered to develop findings when the agreement says so. The manager asked for comments, not findings.

tips: Eliminate: C, because criteria may be left out of advisory work by agreement, and D, because evidence-based findings may be left out the same way.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 13.2 excuses a formal, documented risk assessment in advisory work, while Standard 13.3 excuses no engagement from approval of its objectives and scope.
Exam cue: advisory work bends in three named requirements: formal risk assessment, criteria, evidence-based findings. The rest of the Standards still applies, approvals included.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. A significant risk met in advisory work
questions.question: Mapping a Durban retailer's refund process under an advisory agreement that excludes findings, internal auditor Thabo determines that one clerk who both approves and pays refunds poses a significant risk. What is Thabo's BEST course?

options.A: Keep to the agreed terms, and propose assurance work on refunds
options.B: Tell the manager informally, and keep it out of the engagement record
options.C: Document the risk, and communicate it as a finding of the engagement
options.D: Stop the mapping, and convert the work into an assurance engagement

questions.key_concept: A significant risk has to be written up and reported as a finding. An advisory agreement can waive gathering evidence for findings, not that duty.
questions.pre_read: The agreement limits what Thabo sets out to look for. Does it also limit what Thabo must do with a significant risk already seen?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 lets an advisory agreement dispense with gathering evidence to develop findings. It does not touch Standard 14.3: once internal auditors determine that the organization faces a significant risk, they record and report it as a finding, and Standard 1.1 forbids leaving pertinent information out. Proposing later assurance work, the closest choice, is sensible but leaves a known significant risk unreported. The agreed terms shape the work, not what must be disclosed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: later assurance work may be worth proposing, but it leaves a significant risk that Thabo has already determined unreported, which Standard 14.3 does not permit.
wrong_explanations.B: Telling the manager is a start, but a significant risk must also be documented. An off-the-record word leaves nothing for the chief audit executive or for later work.
wrong_explanations.D: Changing the type of engagement is not Thabo's call alone: changes to objectives and scope need the chief audit executive's approval. Reporting the risk needs no conversion.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a significant risk must be documented as well as communicated, and D, because converting the engagement needs the chief audit executive's approval and is not needed to report.
Final two: C beats A because proposing later assurance leaves a significant risk already determined unreported; Standard 14.3 has no exception for advisory work.
Exam cue: an advisory agreement can narrow what you look for, not what you must report. A significant risk you have determined is documented and communicated.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. A request to swap assurance for advice
questions.question: A Hungarian logistics firm's operations director asks chief audit executive Eszter to replace the planned warehouse-safety assurance engagement with advice on a safety redesign. What do the Standards MOST clearly require of Eszter?

options.A: Agree the nature and scope of the advice with the director
options.B: Discuss with the board and senior management whether the mandate still fits
options.C: Tell the board and senior management of the conflicting demands
options.D: Approve the swap as a change to the engagement's objectives and scope

questions.key_concept: Replacing planned assurance with advisory work is a conflicting demand. The board and senior management must hear of it from the chief audit executive.
questions.pre_read: The director is asking for more than advice: an engagement in the approved plan would disappear. Who needs to hear about that?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 names this case. The chief audit executive must tell the board and senior management in good time of conflicting demands for services, and one example it gives is a request to swap a planned assurance engagement for an advisory one. The board approved the plan and would lose assurance on warehouse safety. Agreeing the advice with the director, the closest choice, suits an ordinary advisory request, not one that displaces planned assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: advisory nature and scope are agreed with the requester, but this request also removes a planned assurance engagement, which is not the director's to settle.
wrong_explanations.B: A mandate discussion follows a change in circumstances that may outgrow the charter. One request to swap engagements does not put the function's authority or role in question.
wrong_explanations.D: The chief audit executive approves objectives and scope inside an engagement. Replacing an engagement in the plan is a plan matter that the board and senior management must hear.

tips: Eliminate: B, because nothing here changes the mandate, and D, because swapping a planned engagement is a plan matter and not a change of scope inside one engagement.
Final two: C beats A because the request displaces assurance in the approved plan; Standard 9.4 makes that a conflicting demand to put before the board and senior management.
Exam cue: an advisory request that adds work is agreed with the requester. One that replaces planned assurance is a conflicting demand for the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. Criteria for a contract compliance audit
questions.question: A Kenyan tea packer's board suspects its freight carrier of overbilling and late deliveries and asks for an assurance engagement. Which criteria BEST fit internal auditor Achieng's assessment of the carrier's invoices and deliveries?

options.A: The rates and delivery windows in the carriage agreement
options.B: The packer's policy for selecting and approving its carriers
options.C: The national regulations on road freight operators
options.D: The rates and delivery times of other carriers nearby

questions.key_concept: Compliance includes keeping to contracts. In a contract compliance audit the agreed terms are the criteria; market rates and internal policies answer other questions.
questions.pre_read: 'Overbilling' and 'late' compared with what? Name the document that says what the carrier promised.
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary counts contracts among the requirements that compliance means keeping to, and Standard 13.4's considerations list contractual obligations as external criteria. Whether the carrier overbilled or delivered late can be judged against the rates and delivery windows it agreed to, which makes this a contract compliance audit. Other carriers' prices, the closest choice, would show whether the deal is competitive, not whether its terms were kept.

wrong_explanations.B: The selection policy is the yardstick for how the packer chooses and approves carriers. It says nothing about what this carrier may bill or when it must deliver.
wrong_explanations.C: Road freight regulations are criteria for a regulatory compliance audit. They do not set the prices and delivery windows agreed between these two parties.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a benchmark against other carriers tests whether the terms are competitive. Overbilling and lateness are measured against what this carrier agreed to.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a selection policy governs how carriers are chosen, and C, because regulations are the yardstick for regulatory compliance and not for agreed prices.
Final two: A beats D because overbilling and lateness mean departing from agreed terms; other carriers' rates show competitiveness, a different question.
Exam cue: name the criteria from the question asked. Kept its promises: the contract. Obeyed the law: the regulation. Good value: a benchmark.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. A Topical Requirement in assurance and advisory work
questions.question: A Latvian bank's internal audit plan includes advisory work on a draft cybersecurity policy; mid-year the board adds an assurance engagement on the payment unit's cybersecurity. How does the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement MOST accurately apply?

options.A: Mandatory for both the policy work and the payment-unit work
options.B: Mandatory for the policy work; recommended for the payment-unit work
options.C: Mandatory for the payment-unit work; not applicable to the policy work
options.D: Mandatory for the payment-unit work; recommended for the policy work

questions.key_concept: A Topical Requirement is mandatory for assurance services on its topic and recommended for advisory services, whether or not the work was first planned.
questions.pre_read: Two things differ between the engagements: the type of service and whether it was planned. Which one sets the Topical Requirement's force?
questions.correct_explanation: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement says assurance services must conform with it, while for advisory services conformance is recommended. It applies when its topic is the subject of a planned engagement, turns up during one, or is requested outside the original plan, so the engagement the board added is covered. The type of service, not the timing, sets its force. 'Not applicable', the closest choice, goes too far: for advisory work, following it is recommended.

wrong_explanations.A: For advisory services conformance is recommended, not mandatory. Assurance services on the topic are the ones that must conform with a Topical Requirement.
wrong_explanations.B: Timing does not decide. A request outside the original plan is one of the three cases in which a Topical Requirement applies, so the added assurance engagement must conform.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the assurance half is right, but a Topical Requirement is not switched off for advisory work on its topic. Following it there is recommended.

tips: Eliminate: A, because conformance is recommended and not mandatory for advisory services, and B, because an assurance engagement added after the plan was set is still covered.
Final two: D beats C because advisory work on the topic is not exempt; the Topical Requirement is recommended there, and mandatory for the assurance engagement.
Exam cue: for a Topical Requirement, ask what kind of service it is, not when the work was planned. Assurance: must conform. Advisory: recommended.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. The objective of an audit of culture
questions.question: After crews hid two near-misses, the board of a Greek ferry line asks its internal audit function for an assurance engagement on safety culture. Which engagement objective fits that request BEST?

options.A: To assess the controls that keep sailings within safety regulations
options.B: To assess how expected safety behavior is set, encouraged and monitored
options.C: To confirm that each crew member completed the safety training
options.D: To measure how satisfied the crews are with their work

questions.key_concept: An audit of culture assesses the governance, risk management and control processes that shape behavior. Training records or a staff survey are only evidence.
questions.pre_read: Assurance is always about governance, risk management and control processes over a subject. What would those be when the subject is behavior?
questions.correct_explanation: By the glossary, assurance concerns the governance, risk management and control processes over a subject, compared with criteria. When the subject is culture, those processes are how leaders set the behavior they expect, encourage it and check on it; Standard 9.1 treats promoting an ethical culture as part of governance. Controls over safety regulations, the closest choice, make a compliance engagement: rules can be met on paper while crews still hide near-misses.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: that objective tests compliance with safety rules. The board asked about behavior, and hidden near-misses can sit beside controls that satisfy the regulations.
wrong_explanations.C: Training completion is one control and one piece of evidence. It shows that crews were told what is expected, not how they behave.
wrong_explanations.D: A satisfaction survey measures how crews feel about their work. It may inform a culture engagement, but it does not assess the processes that shape behavior.

tips: Eliminate: C, because training completion is one piece of evidence and not the objective, and D, because satisfaction is not the same thing as behavior.
Final two: B beats A because the board asked about culture; controls over regulations make a compliance engagement, while culture is about how expected behavior is set, encouraged and monitored.
Exam cue: for any assurance engagement, name the subject, then ask what governance, risk management and control processes sit over it. For culture, the subject is behavior.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. An audit of the management reporting process
questions.question: A Chilean courier firm's board pack shows 97% on-time delivery, yet customer complaints about lateness keep rising. Which internal audit engagement would MOST directly tell the board whether it can rely on the pack's figure?

options.A: An operational audit of the delivery process
options.B: A compliance audit of delivery terms in customer contracts
options.C: An audit of the firm's management reporting process
options.D: A financial audit of delivery revenue and costs

questions.key_concept: An audit of the management reporting process asks whether decision makers get reliable information: how figures are sourced, compiled and reviewed before they are reported.
questions.pre_read: Is the board asking why deliveries are late, or whether the number it was given can be trusted?
questions.correct_explanation: The board's question is about the figure, not the deliveries. Standard 9.1 names reliable financial and operational information as a key risk area, and an audit of the management reporting process examines how such figures are sourced, compiled and reviewed before they reach decision makers. An operational audit, the closest choice, would show how well deliveries run and why some are late, but not why the pack says 97%.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an operational audit assesses how effectively and efficiently deliveries run. It would explain lateness, not whether the reported figure is reliable.
wrong_explanations.B: A contract compliance audit tests whether agreed terms were kept. It could find late deliveries, but it does not examine how the board's figure is produced.
wrong_explanations.D: A financial audit looks at financial information and the controls behind it. On-time delivery is operational information, and its reporting is the question here.

tips: Eliminate: B, because contract terms are a different yardstick from the reported figure, and D, because on-time delivery is operational and not financial information.
Final two: C beats A because the board asked whether it can rely on the figure; an operational audit explains performance, while the reporting audit tests the number's reliability.
Exam cue: name the engagement from the question the board asks. How well does it run: operational. Was a rule kept: compliance. Can we trust the report: management reporting.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. Internal audit's financial work and the external opinion
questions.question: A Mongolian cashmere exporter's lenders require accounts carrying an independent opinion written for them; its internal audit function audits revenue reporting for the board. Whose work do the lenders' terms MOST clearly call for?

options.A: The external auditor's, engaged to report on the full statements
options.B: The internal audit function's, widened to cover every account
options.C: The finance function's, with the finance director's sign-off
options.D: The audit committee's, as the body overseeing financial reporting

questions.key_concept: Internal audit's financial work gives the board and management assurance. An independent opinion on the accounts for outside parties comes from the external auditor.
questions.pre_read: Who is the opinion written for: people inside the organization, or people outside it?
questions.correct_explanation: By the Purpose of Internal Auditing the function serves the board and management, and its financial engagements give them assurance. The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model places external audit outside the three lines: it gives an independent opinion, usually on the financial statements, to creditors and other outside stakeholders. Lenders ask for that. Widening internal audit's scope, the closest choice, changes coverage, not whom the function serves.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: wider scope would cover more accounts, but the function would still serve the board and management. The lenders want an opinion from outside the organization.
wrong_explanations.C: Finance prepares the accounts and its director signs them as management. That sign-off is management's own statement, not an independent opinion on it.
wrong_explanations.D: An audit committee oversees; it does not perform audit work or issue an opinion on the accounts. The lenders want the work of an independent auditor.

tips: Eliminate: C, because finance cannot give an independent opinion on accounts it prepares, and D, because the audit committee oversees audit work and does not perform it.
Final two: A beats B because the lenders are outside stakeholders; internal audit's financial assurance serves the board and management, however wide its scope.
Exam cue: ask who relies on the work. The board and management: internal audit. Creditors, regulators or the public: the external auditor's opinion.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Recognizing internal benchmarking
questions.question: A Vietnamese furniture maker's operations head asks internal audit, as advisory work, why its plants scrap so much timber. Which analysis by internal auditor Khanh would MOST accurately be called internal benchmarking?

options.A: Comparing scrap rates with those of other furniture makers
options.B: Comparing this year's scrap rates with last year's
options.C: Comparing scrap rates with the target in the production plan
options.D: Comparing scrap rates across the maker's three plants

questions.key_concept: Internal benchmarking compares the same measure between areas of one organization. Comparing with similar organizations is external benchmarking; management decides what to change.
questions.pre_read: Benchmarking needs a comparison partner. For the internal kind, where does that partner sit?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2's considerations list internal benchmarking, a comparison between areas of the same organization, and external benchmarking, a comparison with similar organizations, as separate analyses. Setting the three plants' scrap rates side by side is the internal kind. Comparing with other furniture makers, the closest choice, is benchmarking too, but the external kind. Either way the auditor explains the differences and management decides what to change.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this is benchmarking, but against similar organizations, which makes it external. The internal kind stays inside one organization.
wrong_explanations.B: Comparing a measure with the same measure in an earlier period is a trend comparison. The partner is the past, not another area.
wrong_explanations.C: Comparing results with a target sets the condition against criteria. That is how a gap is found, not benchmarking between areas.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a comparison with last year is a trend analysis, and C, because a comparison with a target sets condition against criteria.
Final two: D beats A because internal benchmarking compares areas inside one organization; comparing with other makers is external benchmarking.
Exam cue: name a comparison by its partner. Another unit: internal benchmarking. Another organization: external benchmarking. An earlier period: trend. A target: criteria.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Advisory work the internal auditors start
questions.question: A Peruvian fishing cooperative's charter covers advisory services, and chief audit executive Milagros believes mapping the catch-payment process would help its manager, who has not asked. What is Milagros's BEST course?

options.A: Hold the idea until the manager or the board requests it
options.B: Map the process now, and give the manager the finished map
options.C: Propose the mapping to the manager and agree on its scope
options.D: Report the unmapped process to the manager as a finding

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors may start advisory work themselves; it need not wait for a request. Its nature and scope are still agreed with the stakeholders concerned.
questions.pre_read: Must advisory work begin with someone else's request? And once begun, who has to agree what it will cover?
questions.correct_explanation: The introduction to Domain V says internal auditors may initiate advisory services as well as perform them on request, and the glossary makes their nature and scope a matter of agreement with the stakeholders concerned. So Milagros can put the idea to the manager and settle with them what the mapping will cover. Waiting for a request, the closest choice, treats advisory work as something others have to start; the Standards do not.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many advisory engagements do start with a request, but the Standards also let internal auditors initiate them. Nothing requires waiting to be asked.
wrong_explanations.B: Advisory nature and scope are subject to agreement with the stakeholders concerned. Mapping first and presenting the result later leaves the manager out of that agreement.
wrong_explanations.D: A finding is a gap between criteria and condition in an engagement. No engagement is under way, and no criterion says the process must be mapped.

tips: Eliminate: B, because advisory scope is agreed before the work and not after it, and D, because a finding needs an engagement and criteria.
Final two: C beats A because internal auditors may initiate advisory services themselves; they still agree the nature and scope with the manager before starting.
Exam cue: advisory work can start from either side. What cannot be skipped is agreeing its nature and scope, and leaving every decision to management.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Taking part in due diligence
questions.question: The chief executive of a Bangladeshi food group asks its internal audit function to take part in due diligence on a planned purchase of a rival. Which description of the function's part is MOST accurate?

options.A: Assurance: it concludes whether the rival's controls are effective
options.B: Advisory: it advises managers on the rival's risks and controls
options.C: A wider role: it needs board-approved safeguards before starting
options.D: Assurance: it tests the group's own controls over acquisitions

questions.key_concept: Due diligence is an advisory service: the internal auditor advises on the target's risks and controls, gives no assurance, and management decides on the deal.
questions.pre_read: A decision is about to be made by management. Is the function asked for confidence against criteria, or for input to that decision?
questions.correct_explanation: The CIA Part 1 syllabus lists due diligence among the advisory services an internal audit function performs, and the glossary defines advisory services as advice given without assurance and without management responsibility. Here the function feeds what it sees of the rival's risks and controls into a decision that stays with management. Concluding that those controls are effective, the closest choice, would be assurance, which needs criteria and enough evidence about another company's processes.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a conclusion on effectiveness is assurance. Due diligence input is advice to those deciding on the purchase, and it claims no assurance over the rival.
wrong_explanations.C: Board-approved safeguards belong to a role beyond internal auditing, such as running a function. Advising a deal team is an advisory engagement, an internal audit service.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing the group's own acquisition controls would be a separate assurance engagement. The chief executive asked for help with this purchase, not an audit of the process.

tips: Eliminate: C, because advising a deal team is an internal audit service and not a wider role, and D, because auditing the group's own acquisition process is a different engagement.
Final two: B beats A because due diligence input is advice for management's decision; concluding that the rival's controls are effective would be assurance, which this work does not give.
Exam cue: when the function helps before a decision, on something not yet the organization's own, think advisory: input on risks and controls, no assurance, management decides.
